definition: Continuing to try with stubborn determination, even when progress is slow or hard.
example: Her dogged practice on the cello through the long winter finally paid off at the spring recital.
nuance: Dogged stresses steady, unglamorous persistence through difficulty; tenacious suggests a firm grip that refuses to let go.
prompt: A local reporter is trying to get answers about a delayed bridge repair.
options: The dogged reporter called the city office every morning for a month until a clerk finally talked.
The dogged reporter dropped the story after one email to the city went unanswered.
The dogged reporter refused to look at any fact that challenged her opinion of the mayor's office.
The dogged reporter was so worn out after her late shift that she dozed off at her desk.
reasons: Calling again and again for weeks despite silence shows stubborn, patient persistence.
Quitting at the first obstacle is the reverse of refusing to give up.
Rigidly clinging to a belief describes being dogmatic, a look-alike word, not dogged.
Being exhausted is dog-tired; dogged is about determination, not fatigue.

practice.prompt: A student is working through a tough chemistry problem set the night before it is due.
options: With dogged effort, Marcus insisted his wrong answers were correct and ignored the teacher's notes.
With dogged effort, Marcus reworked each problem until his answers matched the key.
With dogged effort, Marcus skimmed the first page and gave up before dinner.
With dogged effort, Marcus guessed at random and happened to get every answer right.
reasons: Stubbornly refusing correction is closed-mindedness, closer to dogmatic than to dogged.
Redoing hard work repeatedly until it comes out right is persistence in the face of difficulty.
Skimming and quitting early shows little effort and no staying power.
Lucky guessing involves no sustained struggle, so the word's sense of grinding effort is missing.
